I. Text Para 3 & Para 4

Para 3▸
The boy later learns what the statuettes meant: the headmaster set them to face misbehaving boys because they stood for the whole of life — Venus (love), the leopard (nature), the Thinker (pure thought).
0:00 / 0:00
Some time later, I learned about these statuettes. The headmaster had placed them where they would face delinquent children, because they symbolized to him the whole of life. The naked lady was Venus. She was Love. She was not worried about the towel. She was just busy being beautiful. The leopard was Nature, and he was being natural. The muscular gentleman was not miserable. He was Rodin's Thinker, an image of pure thought.
Paraphrase
Some time later I understood what those statuettes meant, and why the headmaster set them facing the boys.

Para 4▸
The narrator explains he was a frequent visitor to the headmaster's study; in modern terms he was 'disintegrated' (maladjusted), and would sink his head and writhe his shoes when caught.
0:00 / 0:00
I had better explain that I was a frequent visitor to the headmaster's study, because of the latest thing I had done or left undone. As we now say, I was not integrated. I was, if anything, disintegrated. Whenever I found myself in a penal position before the headmaster's desk I would sink my head, and writhe one shoe over the other.

Verb Phrases (1) · Noun Phrases (4) · Collocations (1)
① Verb Phrases
sink one's headVerb Phrase
to lower one's head, esp. from shame or nervousness

TextWhenever I found myself in a penal position before the headmaster's desk I would sink my head, and writhe one shoe over the other.
每当我发现自己站在校长办公桌前准备受罚的时候，我就低下头，一只鞋在另一只鞋上不安地蹭来蹭去。
E.g.Ashamed of his mistake, he sank his head and said nothing.
他因错误羞愧地低下头，一言不发。
② Noun Phrases

pure thoughtNoun Phrase

E.g.As a frequent visitor to this library, she knows every corner of it well.

TextWhenever I found myself in a penal position before the headmaster's desk I would sink my head, and writhe one shoe over the other.

used to suggest that the opposite of what was just said may be true

TextAs we now say, I was not integrated. I was, if anything, disintegrated.

IV. Paraphrase （2）

Para 3 · Para 4
Para 3
Some time later, I learned about these statuettes. The headmaster had placed them where they would face delinquent children, because they symbolized to him the whole of life. The naked lady was Venus. She was Love. She was not worried about the towel. She was just busy being beautiful. The leopard was Nature, and he was being natural. The muscular gentleman was not miserable. He was Rodin's Thinker, an image of pure thought.
Some time later I understood what those statuettes meant. The headmaster had put them where they would look at badly-behaved boys, because to him they stood for the whole of life. The naked lady was Venus, the goddess of love; she was not bothered about the towel but was simply occupied with being beautiful. The leopard represented Nature and was acting naturally. The muscular man was not unhappy; he was Rodin's Thinker, a picture of pure thought.
Notes
  • statuettes 为 statuette 的复数；face 此处作“面对／面向”（face delinquent children＝正对着那些有违法倾向的孩子），非“脸”
  • symbolize “象征”，过去式 symbolized；be busy being beautiful “只顾着美着”
  • image of pure thought “纯粹思考的化身”。此段以冷静口吻重写 Para 2 雕像的“panic / miserable”，呼应男孩不动声色的反讽视角
Para 4
I had better explain that I was a frequent visitor to the headmaster's study, because of the latest thing I had done or left undone. As we now say, I was not integrated. I was, if anything, disintegrated. Whenever I found myself in a penal position before the headmaster's desk I would sink my head, and writhe one shoe over the other.
I should explain that I often had to go to the headmaster's study, on account of something I had just done or failed to do. In today's terms, I was not well-adjusted; if anything, I was the opposite — badly maladjusted. Each time I ended up standing like a punished child in front of his desk, I would drop my head and rub one shoe against the other.
Notes
  • had better “最好还是”（表建议，后接动词原形）
  • the latest thing I had done or left undone “我最近做的或没做的事”（left undone＝未做）
  • integrated “融入集体、适应良好的”，disintegrated 为其反义，构成反义对照兼文字游戏（antithesis / paronomasia）
  • penal “受罚的”（a penal position 喻“如受审般”），此处非“刑事的”本义；writhe “（紧张地）扭动”

V. Translation （2）

Para 3 · Para 4
Para 3
Some time later, I learned about these statuettes. The headmaster had placed them where they would face delinquent children, because they symbolized to him the whole of life. The naked lady was Venus. She was Love. She was not worried about the towel. She was just busy being beautiful. The leopard was Nature, and he was being natural. The muscular gentleman was not miserable. He was Rodin's Thinker, an image of pure thought.
后来我才知道这几个雕像是怎么回事。校长之所以把它们放在那儿，让它们冲着犯了错误的孩子们，是因为这些雕像对于他来说象征着生活的全部。那裸体妇人是女神维纳斯，她是爱的化身。她并不是在为随时可能滑落的浴巾而担忧，她只是忙于展现自己的美。那豹子代表自然，它是在忙着展现自己的自然风采。那肌肉发达的男子也并不痛苦悲惨，他是罗丹的雕塑“思想者”，是代表纯粹思维的光辉形象。
Notes
  • “小雕像”← statuettes（与 Para 2 呼应）
  • “正对着”← face（面对，非“脸”）
  • “象征着生活的全部”← symbolized to him the whole of life
  • “纯粹思考的化身”← an image of pure thought（Rodin's Thinker＝罗丹《思想者》）
Para 4
I had better explain that I was a frequent visitor to the headmaster's study, because of the latest thing I had done or left undone. As we now say, I was not integrated. I was, if anything, disintegrated. Whenever I found myself in a penal position before the headmaster's desk I would sink my head, and writhe one shoe over the other.
在这里我得向大家解释一下，由于我不是做了不该做的事情，就是该做的什么事情没有做，因此我就成了校长办公室的常客。用我们现在的话说，我和周围不是很合拍，实际上，正相反，应该说我是一个出格调皮的孩子。所以，每当我发现自己站在校长办公桌前准备受罚的时候，我就低下头，一只鞋在另一只鞋上不安地蹭来蹭去。
Notes
  • “常客”← a frequent visitor
  • “合群／不合群”← integrated / disintegrated（反义文字游戏：integrated 与 disintegrated 仅前缀相反，构成对照）
  • “受罚般的处境”← a penal position（喻校长桌前的紧张）
  • “一只鞋在另一只上蹭来蹭去”← writhe one shoe over the other（writhe 描写紧张小动作）

VI. Culture Notes （2）

Venus · Rodin's Thinker
Venus（维纳斯）
Venus is the Goddess of Love and Beauty in Roman mythology, but here it refers to the Greek statue of the goddess stored in the Louvre in Paris. It was badly damaged but immediately recognizable by its missing arms.
（维纳斯：罗马神话中的爱与美之女神；文中指收藏于巴黎卢浮宫的希腊雕像《米洛的维纳斯》，虽双臂残缺，却一眼可辨。）
Venus de Milo (Aphrodite of Milos), Louvre Museum, Paris
Rodin's Thinker（罗丹《思想者》）
Auguste Rodin (1840—1917) was a French sculptor, considered to be one of the greatest sculptors of his time, whose most famous works are The Thinker and The Kiss.
（奥古斯特·罗丹，法国雕塑家，被誉为同时代最伟大的雕塑家之一；代表作《思想者》与《吻》。）
Le Penseur (The Thinker), Auguste Rodin
Le Baiser (The Kiss), Auguste Rodin
Auguste Rodin (1840–1917) — portrait photograph
